metadata.name: sed
metadata.description: Stream editor for filtering and transforming text

installation.note: sed is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: sed (stream editor) performs text transformations on input streams. It reads input line by line, applies commands, and outputs results. Most commonly used for find-and-replace operations, but can do much more. Essential for text processing, script automation, and batch file editing.
when_to_use: Find and replace text in files

syntax.description: Apply COMMAND to FILE(s) or standard input. Commands are specified in single quotes. Most common: s/pattern/replacement/ for substitution.

misconceptions.title: sed modifies files by default
misconceptions.reality: sed outputs to stdout by default - original file is unchanged. Use -i flag to modify files in-place.
misconceptions.tip: sed outputs to stdout by default. Use sed -i to modify files. Always test without -i first.

misconceptions.title: sed only does find-and-replace
misconceptions.misconception: sed is only for replacing text
misconceptions.reality: sed can delete lines, print specific lines, insert text, transform text, and much more. It's a powerful stream editor.
misconceptions.tip: sed does much more than replace - can delete, print, insert, transform. Learn basic commands: s (substitute), d (delete), p (print).

common_pitfalls.issue: Forgetting -i and expecting file to change
common_pitfalls.description: Running sed without -i and wondering why file didn't change
common_pitfalls.solution: sed outputs to stdout by default. Use sed -i to modify files. Test without -i first to see output.

common_pitfalls.description: Special regex characters in patterns need escaping
common_pitfalls.solution: Escape special characters: sed 's/\./dot/g' (escapes dot). Or use different delimiter: sed 's|old|new|g'.

common_pitfalls.issue: Using -i without backup on important files
common_pitfalls.solution: Use sed -i.bak to create backup, or test without -i first. Be careful with -i on important files.

best_practices: Test sed commands without -i first to verify output
Use sed -i.bak to create backups when modifying files
Escape special regex characters or use different delimiters
Use 'g' flag for global replacement (all occurrences)
Combine with other commands: cat file.txt | sed 's/old/new/g'
Use sed for simple text transformations, awk for complex processing
performance_tips: sed is very fast for text processing
Efficient for large files - processes line by line
Use sed for simple operations, awk for complex ones

additional_notes.default_behavior: sed outputs to stdout by default - original file unchanged. Use -i to modify files.
additional_notes.common_commands: Common: s (substitute), d (delete), p (print). Most common: s/old/new/g for find-and-replace.
additional_notes.delimiters: Forward slash is default delimiter, but can use others: sed 's|old|new|g' or sed 's#old#new#g'
additional_notes.regex: sed uses regular expressions - escape special characters or use different delimiters
additional_notes.common_patterns: Very common: sed 's/old/new/g' (replace), sed -i 's/old/new/g' file (modify), sed '/pattern/d' (delete lines)
